---
title: "09 — Transforms on Subsets and Divisors"
---

This chapter is about changing coordinates. A convolution that appears
quadratic often becomes pointwise multiplication after the correct transform.
The central habit is to identify the relation among indices: subset inclusion,
divisibility, or the Boolean group under XOR. The loops are short; the hard part
is proving which operation the statement is actually combining.

Unless a section says otherwise, array values live in a commutative ring. The
zeta/Möbius stages themselves use only addition and subtraction; a convolution
also needs the pointwise products in the transformed coordinates to make sense.

## Prerequisites, notation, and learning objectives

Read [sets and induction](../00-prerequisite-audit/chapter.qmd),
[divisor sums](../02-multiplicative-number-theory/chapter.qmd), and
[modular units](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd). You should learn to derive
the transform from the index relation, prove the inverse, distinguish union
from disjoint union, and choose exact stage orders for divisor transforms.

The universe is $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, subsets are masks $0,\ldots,2^n-1$,
and $|S|$ is the number of set bits. A **poset** is a set with a reflexive,
antisymmetric, transitive relation; subset inclusion and positive divisibility
are examples. A zeta transform sums over predecessors in that relation.
Complexities count ring operations and storage in ring elements, not bit costs
for arbitrarily large integers.

## 1. Subset zeta and Möbius transforms

For a function $f[S]$ on subsets of an $n$-element universe, the **subset zeta
transform** changes coordinates from “exactly set $T$” to “some subset of $S$”:

$$F[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T].$$

For example, if $f[T]$ counts objects whose feature set is exactly $T$, then
$F[S]$ counts objects using only features in $S$. Process one bit at a time,
adding the state without the current bit into the state with it; invert by
subtracting in the same schedule. After processing bits $0,\ldots,i$, the
current value has summed over all ways of deleting those processed bits. This
induction invariant explains the transform—not merely its loop pattern.

More precisely, after a set $B$ of bits is processed, the value at $S$ is
$\sum_{T\subseteq S,\ S\setminus T\subseteq B}f[T]$. The next bit chooses
whether it is deleted, partitioning the allowed terms into two disjoint cases.
For two bits and input $f[\varnothing],f[\{0\}],f[\{1\}],f[\{0,1\}]
=(1,2,3,4)$, processing bit 0 gives $(1,3,3,7)$, then bit 1 gives
$(1,3,4,10)$. Inversion by subtraction recovers the original four entries.

Both take $O(n2^{n})$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory. The inverse works because the
Möbius function of the Boolean lattice is
$\mu(T,S)=(-1)^{|S\setminus T|}$. The bits may be processed in any order because
their stages commute. Keep one bit as the outer stage, however, and invert each
butterfly $(a,b)\mapsto(a,a+b)$ with $(a,b)\mapsto(a,b-a)$; changing which member
of the pair receives the update changes the transform.

The **superset** variants switch the condition and, for masks `s` without bit
`b`, update `f[s] += f[s | (1<<b)]`. Recognition signals include “sum over all
submasks/supermasks”, compatibility masks, and inclusion–exclusion over missing
features.

### OR and AND convolution

For $h[S]=\sum_{A\cup B=S}f[A]g[B]$, subset-zeta both arrays, multiply
pointwise, then subset-Möbius. At a fixed $S$, the product is

$$\left(\sum_{A\subseteq S}f[A]\right)\left(\sum_{B\subseteq S}g[B]\right),$$

which counts all pairs whose union is **contained** in $S$. Möbius inversion
turns “contained in” back into “equal to,” leaving exactly $A\cup B=S$. For
$A\cap B=S$, use superset-zeta instead. Complexity is $O(n2^n)$.

## 2. XOR convolution and FWT

XOR masks form the group $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^{n}$: every mask is its own
inverse. Its characters are the plus/minus functions
$\chi_k(x)=(-1)^{\langle k,x\rangle}$. They turn a shift by XOR into a
multiplicative sign, which is why

$$\widehat f[k]=\sum_x f[x]\chi_k(x),\qquad
\widehat{f *_\oplus g}[k]=\widehat f[k]\widehat g[k].$$

The Walsh–Hadamard butterfly evaluates these characters recursively.

Here $\langle k,x\rangle=\sum_{b=0}^{n-1}k_bx_b\pmod2$ is the parity of
common set bits. A **character** turns the group operation into multiplication:
$\chi_k(a\mathbin\oplus b)=\chi_k(a)\chi_k(b)$, since bit parities add.
Consequently, if $h[s]=\sum_{a\oplus b=s}f[a]g[b]$, then

$$\widehat h[k]=\sum_{a,b}f[a]g[b]\chi_k(a\oplus b)
=\left(\sum_a f[a]\chi_k(a)\right)
 \left(\sum_b g[b]\chi_k(b)\right).$$

For inversion, consider $\sum_k\chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$.
If $x=y$, all $2^n$ terms are one. If $x\ne y$, pick a differing bit;
pair each $k$ with the mask toggling that bit. Their signs are opposite and
cancel. Applying the transform twice therefore gives $2^nf$.
Separating frequency masks by one bit gives the butterfly
$(a,b)\mapsto(a+b,a-b)$, and $n$ stages cost $O(n2^n)$.

For an array of length $N=2^n$, XOR inversion divides by $N$. Thus the
coefficient ring must make $N$ invertible; over a field this is equivalent to
characteristic not two. Under an odd prime modulus multiply by $N^{-1}$. With
integers, transform, multiply using a wide type, then divide exactly on inversion.
OR/AND FWT uses triangular butterflies and has no normalization.

In characteristic two, the length-two transform sends both $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
to $(1,1)$, so it loses information. There is no inverse scaling that repairs
that collision. Over integers, exact final division is valid, but intermediate
transformed products can be much larger than final coefficients.

**Worked example.** With $f[0]=1,f[1]=2$ and $g[0]=3,g[1]=4$, the XOR convolution is $[1·3+2·4, 1·4+2·3]=[11,10]$. Their transforms are $[3,-1]$ and $[7,-1]$; pointwise product $[21,1]$, inverse butterfly gives $[11,10]$.

## 3. Subset convolution

The disjoint-union convolution is

$$h[S]=\sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]g[S\setminus T].$$

Plain enumeration costs $O(3^{n})$. Split each array by rank: $f_k[S]=f[S]$ if $|S|=k$, else zero. Zeta-transform every rank, form

$$H_k[S]=\sum_{i=0}^{k} F_i[S]G_{k-i}[S],$$

Möbius-transform each rank, and take $h[S]=H_{|S|}[S]$. After inversion, the
rank-$k$ entry contains pairs with $A\cup B=S$ and $|A|+|B|=k$. Selecting
$k=|S|$ forces $|A\cap B|=0$ because
$|A|+|B|=|A\cup B|+|A\cap B|$. This is why overlapping operands disappear.
Time is $O(n^{2}2^{n})$ and memory is $O(n2^{n})$.

Use ranks $0\le k\le n$ and inner indices $0\le i\le k$ for the product;
ranks above $n$ cannot affect a requested rank $|S|\le n$. However, before
Möbius inversion do **not** clear entries merely because $k>|S|$:
they contain overlapping pairs which must cancel at larger masks. For example,
two copies of singleton $\{0\}$ contribute rank two at mask $\{0\}$ and
also at $\{0,1\}$ after zeta. Inversion subtracts the former from the latter.
Prematurely deleting the former leaves a false disjoint contribution.

For $S=\{0,1\}$, the four summands are

$$
f[\varnothing]g[S]+f[\{0\}]g[\{1\}]
+f[\{1\}]g[\{0\}]+f[S]g[\varnothing].
$$

The rank index is what distinguishes these disjoint splits from OR convolution,
which would also admit overlapping pairs such as $(S,S)$.

Use it when the transition partitions a set into two labeled, disjoint parts and $n$ is around 20. If one side can be enumerated sparsely, $O(3^{n})$ may be smaller and easier.

At $n=20$, one rank array of 32-bit entries occupies
$21\cdot2^{20}\cdot4=88{,}080{,}384$ bytes, or 84 MiB. Three such arrays
need 252 MiB before other storage. Check the actual number of live arrays and
memory limit; the asymptotic space bound alone does not promise feasibility.

## 4. Divisor-poset transforms

On positive integers ordered by divisibility, the same idea replaces “subset”
by “divisor”:

$$F[x]=\sum_{d\mid x}f[d],\qquad G[x]=\sum_{x\mid m}f[m].$$

For arrays up to $N$, divisor zeta uses $f[ip]\mathrel{+}=f[i]$ for every prime
$p$ and $ip\le N$. Traverse $i$ upward in the forward stage and downward while
subtracting in the inverse, so chains $i,ip,ip^2,\ldots$ accumulate and undo
correctly. Multiple zeta uses the reversed update $f[i]\mathrel{+}=f[ip]$:
traverse $i$ downward in the forward stage and upward while subtracting in the
inverse. A linear-sieve list of primes makes the structural analogy with subset
bits explicit.

In each prime stage, the exact range is $1\le i\le\lfloor N/p\rfloor$;
prime stages cover every prime $p\le N$. For the $p=2$ chain $1,2,4$,
values $(a,b,c)$ become $(a,a+b,a+b+c)$ when the updates run upward.
To undo them, subtract the entry at 2 from that at 4 first, then the entry
at 1 from that at 2. Forward descending order would produce $(a,a+b,b+c)$,
omitting $a$ from index 4.

After processing a prime set $P$, divisor zeta at $x$ sums $f[d]$ over exactly
those divisors $d\mid x$ for which every prime factor of $x/d$ lies in $P$.
Each prime stage adds all choices of that prime's exponent once, by its chain.
Unique prime factorization makes the stages commute; inverse stages must undo
the chain dependence within each prime.

For LCM convolution, “both inputs divide $x$” is the transformed condition,
so divisor zeta, pointwise multiply, then invert. For GCD convolution, the
natural condition is “both inputs are multiples of $x$,” so use sums over
multiples. The update directions above matter because an in-place stage must
first accumulate a whole prime-power chain and later undo it in the reverse
dependency order. Complexity is
$O(N\log\log N)$ with prime-stage transforms (or $O(N\log N)$ with direct
divisor loops).

Preconditions: indices start at 1; define deliberately whether zero exists. $\gcd(0,x)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(0,x)$ make zero a special element, so most contest implementations handle it separately.

The LCM output here is restricted to $1,\ldots,N$. Pairs whose LCM exceeds
$N$ contribute nowhere in that output. For any retained $x$, both operands
divide $x$ and hence already lie in the retained range, so the divisor-zeta
identity is unaffected by discarding those large outputs. For GCD convolution,
all positive-input pairs have a GCD inside the range.

## 5. Pitfalls and decision guide

- `A | B`, `A & B`, and `A ^ B` require three different transforms; visual similarity is not algebraic equivalence.
- Möbius inversion must be performed in the same ring as the sums. Under a modulus, normalize subtraction.
- $O(n^{2} 2^{n})$ subset convolution becomes memory-bound first. Use contiguous rank-major storage.
- SOS DP may need only one transformed array, not a convolution. Do not pay for an inverse you do not need.
- For counting reachable XORs, a linear basis can beat FWT; FWT is appropriate when multiplicities/distributions matter for every XOR value.

## 6. Solved exercises

### A. Union is not disjoint union

Let $f[\{0\}]=g[\{0\}]=1$ and all other entries vanish on a two-element
universe. Find the OR and disjoint-union convolutions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
There is only one ordered pair with nonzero weight; inspect its intersection.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
OR convolution has value one at $\{0\}$, since the union of the singleton
with itself is that singleton. Subset convolution is zero everywhere because
the pair overlaps. In the ranked method it has rank two and union size one,
so it is rejected only when selecting the final rank $|S|$ after inversion.
:::

### B. Count AND-zero subsequences

For input masks $(1,2,3)$ on two bits, count nonempty subsequences with AND zero.
Derive the formula from transformed counts, not by guessing alternating signs.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Let $c[S]$ count inputs containing all bits of $S$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In mask order 0,1,2,3, $c=(3,2,2,1)$. A subsequence whose AND contains $S$
chooses any nonempty subset of those occurrences, so $F[S]=2^{c[S]}-1$
is the superset zeta of the exact-AND distribution. Möbius inversion at zero
gives $7-3-3+1=2$. They are the occurrences $(1,2)$ and $(1,2,3)$.
In general, compute $c$ in $O(n2^n)$, then sum
$\sum_S(-1)^{|S|}(2^{c[S]}-1)$. Repeated values remain distinct occurrences.
:::

### C. Recover exact gcd counts

Both operands are independently chosen from $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Find the numbers
of ordered pairs with gcd 1, 2, 3, and 4.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Pairs with both operands divisible by $d$ number $\lfloor4/d\rfloor^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $h[d]$ count exact gcd $d$. Then $\lfloor4/d\rfloor^2=\sum_{d\mid m}h[m]$.
Descending subtraction gives $h[4]=1$, $h[3]=1$, $h[2]=4-h[4]=3$,
and $h[1]=16-h[2]-h[3]-h[4]=11$. The values sum to all 16 pairs.
This is multiple-zeta inversion; pointwise squaring counts independent ordered
choices and would need correction for unordered pairs or distinct indices.
:::

## 7. Practice, in order

Labels: **Foundation** isolates one idea; **Advanced** combines it; **Mastery** requires recognition; **Capstone** is suitable for team practice. All statements below are available in English.

1. **Foundation — [Compatible Numbers, CF 165E](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/165/E)** (English). Superset/subset SOS DP. [Official tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/4124).
   - Prerequisite: bitmasks.
   - Why: the canonical “find a disjoint present mask” transform.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. A number compatible with $x$ is a submask of the complement of $x$.
   2. Store any present witness, then propagate witnesses from submasks.
   3. Propagate any present witness from submasks. This uses the same dependency
      order as zeta but is not an invertible additive transform; no inverse is needed.
   </details>

2. **Advanced — [Jzzhu and Numbers, CF 449D](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/449/D)** (English). Superset zeta plus inclusion–exclusion. [Official tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/13112).
   - Prerequisite: counting subsequences, Möbius inversion.
   - Why: converts AND-zero into counts of elements containing each mask.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Count subsequences whose AND contains $S$.
   2. If $c[S]$ input values contain $S$, there are $2^{c[S]}-1$ nonempty choices.
   3. Möbius-invert, or take the alternating sum by popcount.
   </details>

3. **Advanced — [Nim Counting, AtCoder ABC212 H](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc212/tasks/abc212_h)** (English). XOR FWT. [Official editorial](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc212/editorial).
   - Prerequisite: modular arithmetic, generating counts by length.
   - Why: forces character-space reasoning rather than treating FWT as a black box.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Winning/losing is determined by the XOR of chosen pile sizes.
   2. Transform the one-choice frequency distribution.
   3. Sum transformed powers for lengths 1 through $N$, invert, and subtract
      the XOR-zero count from all $K+\cdots+K^N$ sequences. At transformed value
      one, the geometric sum is $N$; do not divide by a vanishing difference.
   </details>

4. **Mastery — [Sum the Fibonacci, CF 914G](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/914/G)** (English). Ranked subset, XOR, and AND convolutions together. [Official tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/57250).
   - Prerequisite: ranked subset convolution and XOR/AND transforms.
   - Why: the explicit disjointness condition changes OR into subset convolution.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Build frequency array $f$. The $a,b$ pair must satisfy $s_a\mathbin\&s_b=0$;
      obtain its union distribution by ranked subset convolution $f*f$.
   2. Obtain the $d,e$ XOR distribution separately. Multiply these distributions
      and the single-element distribution pointwise by the corresponding Fibonacci values.
   3. AND-convolve the three weighted distributions and sum outputs at powers
      of two. The statement counts ordered five-tuples of indices, allowing
      repeated indices: no symmetry division belongs in these convolutions.
   </details>

## 8. Reference sheet

| Index relation | Transform or method | Time | Extra algebra |
|---|---|---|---|
| $A\cup B=S$ | Subset zeta / product / inverse | $O(n2^n)$ | None beyond ring operations |
| $A\cap B=S$ | Superset zeta / product / inverse | $O(n2^n)$ | None beyond ring operations |
| $A\oplus B=S$ | Walsh–Hadamard | $O(n2^n)$ | $2^n$ unit, or exact integer division |
| $A\sqcup B=S$ | Ranked subset convolution | $O(n^22^n)$ | Keep overlap ranks until inversion |
| $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)=s$ | Divisor zeta | $O(N\log\log N)$ | Positive indices; output truncated at $N$ |
| $\gcd(a,b)=s$ | Multiple zeta | $O(N\log\log N)$ | Positive indices |

The common proof strategy is to transform “exactly this result” into a sum
over “results below/above this index,” factor the independent choices, and
invert. XOR instead uses multiplicative signs of a group. Check which proof
applies before calling a library routine.
